why_how.text: Shapes tell you the kind of message: vertical rectangles state the law, horizontal ones inform, diamonds warn and pentagons mark schools.
Regulatory signs state the law and must be obeyed, including speed limits that assume good weather.

scenario.text: Dev drives at the posted limit during heavy rain.

reasoning.text: A speed limit sign states the maximum legal speed in good weather, and rain, snow or ice can earn a ticket even at or below the posted number.

result.text: Dev can still be ticketed, so he slows below the posted limit for the rain.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you cannot be ticketed while driving at or below the posted limit.

correction.text: The posted limit is the maximum in good weather, and rain, snow or ice can earn a ticket even at or below the posted number.

memory_support.text: Tall rules, wide guides, diamonds warn, pentagons school.

prompt.text: Dev drives at the posted limit in heavy rain. Can he be ticketed?

answer.text: Yes. The limit is the maximum for good weather, and rain can earn a ticket even at or below it.

rationale.text: A speed limit sign states the maximum legal speed in good weather, so bad weather can make the posted speed unlawful.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on sign shapes and basic regulatory signs. The shape of a sign tells you what kind of message it carries before you read a word of it. In this lesson we will sort out rectangles, diamonds and five-sided pentagons, then look at regulatory signs, which state the law and must be obeyed. We will cover the red circle with a slash, speed limit signs and how weather affects them, electronic limits that change, and three signs about direction: Do Not Enter, Wrong Way and One Way. The first two tell you that you are heading into opposing traffic, and the third only tells you the legal direction of flow.

Vertical rectangles instruct or state the law, while horizontal rectangles give directions or information. Diamonds warn of special conditions or hazards ahead, so when you see one, slow down, drive cautiously and stand ready to stop. Five-sided pentagons mark school zones and school crossings, sometimes paired so that the second sign shows the crosswalk itself. Learn the four shapes as a set, because each one tells you the job of the sign. A tall rectangle is a rule, a wide rectangle is guidance, a diamond is a warning, and a pentagon means a school. The shape of the sign comes first, and the words on it then tell you the details.

lines.text: Red circle with slash means NO.

narration.text: Regulatory signs state the law, and they must be obeyed. Many of them use a red circle with a slash across it. That circle and slash mean no, and the symbol inside names what is banned. So a red slash over a turning arrow bans that turn, and a red slash over another symbol bans whatever the symbol shows. This is one of the most useful patterns to learn, because once you know it, you can read many regulatory signs from the symbol alone. Remember the shape rule from the last slide: regulatory instructions usually appear on vertical rectangles, and the red slash is a common way those signs say no.

lines.text: Limit: maximum legal speed in good weather.
Some roads post electronic limits that change.
Rain, snow or ice: ticket possible at or below the limit.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A speed limit sign states the maximum legal speed in good weather. It is not a promise that the posted number is always legal. Rain, snow or ice can earn a ticket even at or below the posted number. Some roads also post electronic limits that change. Put the two kinds side by side: fixed posted limits hold in good weather, while electronic limits on some roads change with weather or traffic. So when the weather turns bad, the posted number is the ceiling, not the target, and driving at it can still bring a ticket. Read every speed limit sign with the conditions around you in mind.

lines.text: Do Not Enter, Wrong Way: heading into opposing traffic.
Slow at once, pull over, turn around with care.
One Way: traffic flows with the arrow.

narration.text: Now three direction signs. Do Not Enter and Wrong Way signs mean you are heading into opposing traffic. Slow at once, pull over and turn around with care. A One Way sign means traffic flows only in the direction of its arrow. The difference is urgency. Do Not Enter and Wrong Way order an immediate slowdown and turnaround, while One Way only reports the legal flow direction. If you ever see a Wrong Way sign facing you, the manual's instructions are clear: slow at once, pull over, and turn around carefully. A One Way sign, by contrast, simply tells you which way the traffic on that road is allowed to move.

Here is a quick check: Dev is driving at exactly the posted speed limit during heavy rain. Can he be ticketed? Work it out before reading on. The answer is yes. A speed limit sign states the maximum legal speed in good weather, and rain, snow or ice can earn a ticket even at or below the posted number. The posted limit does not change just because it is raining; it simply stops being a safe guide to what is legal. Dev should slow below the posted limit for the conditions. If you answered no because he was not over the limit, remember that the limit assumes good weather.

To close the lesson: vertical rectangles state instructions or the law, and horizontal rectangles give directions or information. Diamonds warn of special conditions or hazards, so slow down and stand ready to stop. Pentagons mark school zones and crossings. Regulatory signs state the law, and a red circle with a slash means no, with the symbol inside naming what is banned. Speed limits are the maximum legal speed in good weather, and bad weather can bring a ticket even at or below them. Do Not Enter and Wrong Way mean turn around with care, and One Way shows the legal direction. The memory line: tall rules, wide guides, diamonds warn, pentagons school.

why_how.text: Turn and passing bans tell you which moves are illegal, and Virginia treats a U-turn as two left turns.
Lane signs assign turns by lane, steer you past obstacles and reserve lanes and spaces for certain users.

scenario.text: Rosa wants to make a U-turn at an intersection where a No Left Turn sign is posted.

reasoning.text: Virginia counts a U-turn as two left turns, so No Left Turn bans U-turns wherever it is posted.

result.text: Rosa does not make the U-turn there.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a No Left Turn sign still allows a U-turn because no U-turn sign is shown.

correction.text: No Left Turn bans both left turns and U-turns, while No U-Turn bans only the U-turn.

prompt.text: Rosa sees a No Left Turn sign. May she make a U-turn there?

answer.text: No. Virginia counts a U-turn as two left turns, so No Left Turn bans it.

rationale.text: No Left Turn bans both left turns and U-turns, while No U-Turn bans only the U-turn.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on turn, passing and lane signs. These are regulatory signs, so they state the law and must be obeyed. We will start with the turn bans, including a Virginia rule about U-turns that surprises many drivers. Then we look at the Do Not Pass sign, the Left Turn Yield on Green sign, and the difference between No Turn on Red and Left Turn Yield on Green. Finally we cover the lane signs: Keep Right, Lane Use Control, High Occupancy Vehicle lanes, and Disabled Parking spaces. Each of these signs either bans a move, assigns a move, or reserves a lane or a space for particular users, and knowing which is which is the skill this lesson builds.

lines.text: No Left Turn: also bans U-turns.
No Right Turn, No U-Turn, No Turn on Red.
No Turn on Red: wait for green.

narration.text: No Left Turn bans left turns. And because Virginia counts a U-turn as two left turns, a No Left Turn sign also bans U-turns wherever it is posted. No Right Turn, No U-Turn and No Turn on Red each ban the named move. Under a No Turn on Red sign, wait for the green signal before turning. Notice that the No Left Turn sign reaches further than its name suggests, because it covers U-turns too. The No U-Turn sign, by contrast, bans only the U-turn. So if you are looking for a place to turn around, a No Left Turn sign rules it out just as clearly as a No U-Turn sign would.

lines.text: No Left Turn bans left turns and U-turns.
No U-Turn bans only the U-turn.

narration.text: Here is the trap: drivers often think that a No Left Turn sign leaves U-turns allowed, because the sign shows a left arrow rather than a U. In Virginia, that is wrong. Virginia counts a U-turn as two left turns, so No Left Turn bans U-turns wherever it is posted. The contrast to remember is this: No Left Turn bans both left turns and U-turns, while No U-Turn bans only the U-turn. On an exam question that shows a No Left Turn sign and asks whether a U-turn is allowed, the answer is no. The memory line for this slide is short and easy to keep: a U-turn is two lefts, so a left-turn ban covers it.

lines.text: Do Not Pass: hold your lane, even when clear.
Left Turn Yield on Green: you lack the right-of-way.
No Turn on Red: wait for green.

narration.text: A Do Not Pass sign opens a no-passing zone. Hold your lane behind the cars ahead, even when the way looks clear. Left Turn Yield on Green tells left-turning drivers at a green light that they lack the right-of-way. Stop, watch for oncoming traffic, and go only with caution. Compare this with No Turn on Red. No Turn on Red holds you until the green signal, while Left Turn Yield on Green lets you turn after stopping and yielding to oncoming traffic. Both signs are about turning at a signal, but one makes you wait for the color to change, and the other lets you go on green as long as you yield first.

lines.text: Keep Right: island, median or barrier ahead.
Lane Use Control: turn where the lane arrow points.
HOV and Disabled Parking reserve lanes and spaces.

narration.text: Keep Right warns of an island, median or barrier ahead, so hold to the side its arrow shows. Lane Use Control signs assign turns by lane: traffic in the lane must turn where the arrow points, including any special permitted movement. So Lane Use Control arrows command the lane's turn, while a Keep Right arrow steers you past an island, median or barrier. High Occupancy Vehicle signs reserve lanes for buses and for vehicles carrying a driver plus at least the posted number of passengers. Disabled Parking signs reserve those spaces for people holding disabled parking permits. Each of these signs reserves, assigns or steers, and each must be obeyed.

Here is a quick check: Rosa wants to make a U-turn at an intersection where a No Left Turn sign is posted. There is no separate No U-Turn sign. May she make the U-turn? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Virginia counts a U-turn as two left turns, so a No Left Turn sign bans U-turns wherever it is posted. The absence of a No U-Turn sign does not matter, because No Left Turn bans both left turns and U-turns. Only the reverse is narrower: a No U-Turn sign by itself bans just the U-turn. Rosa should continue and find a place where turning around is allowed.

lines.text: Do Not Pass: hold your lane.

narration.text: To close the lesson: No Left Turn bans left turns and, because a U-turn counts as two left turns, U-turns too. No Right Turn, No U-Turn and No Turn on Red each ban the named move, and under No Turn on Red you wait for green. A Do Not Pass sign means hold your lane, even when the way looks clear. Left Turn Yield on Green means you lack the right-of-way, so yield before turning. Keep Right steers you past an island, median or barrier, and Lane Use Control arrows tell you where the lane must turn. HOV lanes are for buses and vehicles with enough passengers, and Disabled Parking is for permit holders.

why_how.text: Warning signs flag possible hazards ahead, so slow down and watch for more signs, signals or work zones.
Speed, control-ahead and lane warnings each tell you what is coming and what to do about it.

scenario.text: Jae drives in the left lane when a lane reduction sign shows the right lane ending.

reasoning.text: At a lane reduction, right-lane drivers merge left when space opens, and left-lane drivers let them in smoothly.

result.text: Jae keeps a steady pace and lets the right-lane drivers merge in smoothly.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking an advisory speed sign sets a new legal limit.

correction.text: An advisory speed recommends the safe exit speed, while a Reduced Speed Limit Ahead sign announces a coming legal limit change.

memory_support.text: Merge shares; reduction means right yields in.

prompt.text: Jae is in the left lane when a lane reduction sign shows the right lane ending. What should he do?

answer.text: Let the right-lane drivers merge in smoothly.

rationale.text: At a lane reduction the ending right lane must merge and the left lane must admit, unlike a merge where both lanes share the duty.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on warning signs for speed, upcoming controls and lane changes. Warning signs flag possible hazards ahead. When you see one, slow down and watch for further markings, signs, signals or work zones. In this lesson we will cover advisory speed signs and the Reduced Speed Limit Ahead sign, the three control-ahead signs, the No Passing Zone sign, and the signs that tell you lanes are joining, ending or splitting. Each warning sign tells you something about the road ahead before you reach it, and the right response almost always begins the same way: slow down, look ahead, and get ready for what the sign describes.

lines.text: Advisory speed: maximum safe speed for a highway exit.
Reduced Speed Limit Ahead: legal limit about to drop.

narration.text: An advisory speed sign states the maximum safe speed for a highway exit. A Reduced Speed Limit Ahead sign means the legal limit is about to drop. These two are easy to confuse because both involve a slower number. The difference is legal force. An advisory speed recommends the safe exit speed, while a Reduced Speed Limit Ahead sign announces a coming legal limit change. So when you see the advisory sign at an exit, it is telling you what speed is safe for that exit. When you see Reduced Speed Limit Ahead, it is telling you that the legal maximum is about to change, so you prepare to slow to the new posted limit.

lines.text: Stop Ahead, Yield Ahead, Signal Ahead.
Slow down and stand ready to stop.
No Passing Zone: hold your lane.

narration.text: Stop Ahead, Yield Ahead and Signal Ahead signs each warn that the named control is coming. Slow down and stand ready to stop. These signs tell you a stop sign, yield sign or signal is coming before you reach it, so you can slow down early. The No Passing Zone sign opens a no-passing zone. Hold your lane behind the cars ahead, even when the way looks clear. Notice that this is the same instruction as the regulatory Do Not Pass sign: in both cases you hold your lane behind the cars ahead. The No Passing Zone sign is the warning-style version, and its message is just as firm as the regulatory one.

lines.text: Reduced Speed Limit Ahead requires a change.
Know which sign you are reading.

narration.text: Here is the trap: an advisory speed sign does not set a new legal limit. It recommends the safe speed for a highway exit. A Reduced Speed Limit Ahead sign, on the other hand, announces that the legal limit itself is about to drop. So an advisory speed recommends the safe exit speed, while Reduced Speed Limit Ahead announces a coming legal limit change. If an exam question asks which sign tells you the legal limit is about to change, the answer is Reduced Speed Limit Ahead. If it asks which sign gives the maximum safe speed for an exit, the answer is the advisory speed sign. Keep recommend and require apart.

lines.text: Merge: two lanes join; both share the duty.
Right lane merges left; left lane lets them in.

narration.text: A Merge sign means two same-direction lanes are joining into one, with drivers in both lanes sharing the duty to merge safely. A lane reduction sign means the right lane ends. Right-lane drivers merge left when space opens, and left-lane drivers let them in smoothly. So the duties differ. At a merge both lanes share the blending duty, while at a lane reduction the ending right lane must merge and the left lane must admit. In both cases the goal is a smooth, safe join, but the lane reduction gives each lane a specific job: the right lane moves over, and the left lane makes room for it to do so.

Divided Highway Begins means the road splits into two one-way roadways. Divided Highway Ends means two-way traffic resumes. Keep right in both cases. Put simply, Divided Highway Begins splits travel into two one-way roadways, while Divided Highway Ends returns both directions to one road. After the Ends sign, two-way traffic resumes on one road. The instruction is the same for both signs, which is to keep right, and that makes this pair easier to remember: the sign tells you whether the road is splitting or rejoining, and you keep right either way.

Here is a quick check: Jae is driving in the left lane when a lane reduction sign shows that the right lane is ending. What should he do? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to let the right-lane drivers merge in smoothly. At a lane reduction, the right-lane drivers merge left when space opens, and the left-lane drivers let them in smoothly. Compare a merge, where two lanes join and drivers in both lanes share the duty to merge safely. At a lane reduction each lane has its own job: the ending right lane must merge, and the left lane must admit. Merge shares; reduction means the right lane yields in.

lines.text: Slow and watch at every warning.

narration.text: To close the lesson: warning signs flag possible hazards, so slow down and watch for more markings, signs, signals or work zones. An advisory speed sign gives the maximum safe speed for a highway exit, and Reduced Speed Limit Ahead means the legal limit is about to drop. Stop Ahead, Yield Ahead and Signal Ahead mean slow down and be ready to stop. A No Passing Zone sign means hold your lane. At a merge both lanes share the duty, and at a lane reduction the right lane merges while the left lane lets it in. Divided Highway Begins splits the road and Divided Highway Ends rejoins it, and you keep right in both cases.

why_how.text: Some warning signs describe the road itself: slippery pavement, low clearance, steep hills and deer.
Others warn of people and slow vehicles: buggies, farm equipment, pedestrians, bicyclists and schoolchildren.

scenario.text: Ana comes up behind a horse-drawn buggy on a rural road.

reasoning.text: Where horse-drawn buggies travel, slow down without sounding the horn and pass with at least three feet of clearance when clear.

result.text: Ana slows, does not use her horn, and passes with at least three feet of clearance once the way is clear.

claim.text: Common mistake: sounding the horn to get a horse-drawn buggy to move over.

correction.text: Near horse-drawn buggies you slow, skip the horn and keep three feet of clearance, while near farm equipment you slow or stop and pass only when clear.

prompt.text: Ana is behind a horse-drawn buggy. Should she sound her horn before passing?

answer.text: No. She slows without sounding the horn and passes with at least three feet of clearance when clear.

rationale.text: Where horse-drawn buggies travel, the manual says slow down without sounding the horn and pass with at least three feet of clearance.

narration.text: Welcome to the last lesson of this section, on road condition and crossing signs. These warning signs tell you about the road surface, the space above you, the grade ahead, and the animals, slow vehicles and people you may meet. We will cover Slippery When Wet, low clearance, hill and deer crossing signs, then the rules for horse-drawn buggies and farm equipment, and finally pedestrian, bicycle, school zone and school crossing signs. Warning signs call for caution, and the specific instruction depends on the sign. But several of these signs add a specific instruction of their own, and those specific instructions are what this lesson is about.

lines.text: Slippery When Wet: slow, no hard braking or sudden moves.
Low clearance: taller than posted cannot pass.
Hill: check brakes. Deer: slow, alert, ready to stop.

narration.text: Slippery When Wet means slow down on wet pavement without hard braking or sudden moves, and leave extra space to the car ahead. A low clearance sign bars any vehicle taller than its posted height from passing under the overpass. A hill sign warns of a steep grade, so check your brakes. A deer crossing sign means slow down, stay alert, and stand ready to stop. Each of these signs describes a physical condition. On slippery pavement the instruction is gentle control and more space. At a low overpass the instruction is about your vehicle's height. On a hill it is your brakes, and in deer country it is alertness and readiness to stop.

lines.text: Buggy: slow, no horn, at least three feet.
Farm equipment: slow or stop, pass only when clear.

narration.text: Here is the trap: horse-drawn buggies and farm equipment are both slow vehicles, but the manual gives them different instructions. Where horse-drawn buggies travel, slow down without sounding the horn, and pass with at least three feet of clearance when clear. Where farm equipment travels, slow down or stop, and pass only when clear. So near horse-drawn buggies you must slow, skip the horn and keep three feet of clearance, while near farm equipment you slow or stop and pass only when clear. The horn rule and the three-foot clearance belong to the buggy. Do not reach for the horn to hurry a buggy along.

lines.text: Pedestrians: slow and prepare to stop.
A second arrow sign may mark the spot.

narration.text: A pedestrian crossing sign calls for slowing and readiness to stop for people walking or riding into your path. A bicycle crossing sign warns of bicycles crossing or riding beside traffic and calls for careful driving. An added arrow sign can identify the location of either crossing. When you see one, expect that someone on foot or on a bicycle may enter the road ahead. The pentagon from the first lesson of this section is the school version of a crossing sign, and the school version adds duties of its own, which come on the next slide. Keep the signs distinct: pedestrian crossings call for slowing and stop readiness, while bicycle crossings call for caution.

lines.text: Obey the limit and the crossing guards.

narration.text: School zone and school crossing signs mean watching for children and standing ready to slow or stop. They also mean obeying the speed limit and the crossing guards. As with other crossings, a second arrow sign sometimes marks the spot. The difference from an ordinary crossing is the extra duties. Pedestrian crossings call for slowing and stop readiness; bicycle crossings call for caution. School zones add watching for children, readiness to slow or stop, and obeying the limit and crossing guards. So at a school crossing, a crossing guard's direction is part of the rule you must follow. Remember the shape as well: school zones and school crossings are marked with five-sided pentagons.

Here is a quick check: Ana comes up behind a horse-drawn buggy on a rural road. Should she sound her horn before passing, and how much room should she give? Work it out before reading on. The answer: no horn, and at least three feet of clearance. Where horse-drawn buggies travel, the manual says slow down without sounding the horn, and pass with at least three feet of clearance when clear. If Ana were behind farm equipment instead, the rule would be to slow down or stop and pass only when clear. The horn rule and the three feet of clearance belong to the buggy rule, not to the farm equipment rule.

To close the section: Slippery When Wet means slow down without hard braking or sudden moves and leave extra space. A low clearance sign bars vehicles taller than the posted height. A hill sign means check your brakes, and a deer crossing sign means slow down, stay alert and be ready to stop. Near horse-drawn buggies, skip the horn and leave at least three feet when passing, and near farm equipment, slow or stop and pass only when clear. Pedestrian crossings mean slow and prepare to stop; bicycle crossings mean drive cautiously. School zones add watching for children and obeying the limit and crossing guards. The memory line: buggies, quiet and three feet.
